title: What Technical Due Diligence Finds When the Deck Says “70% Automated” — Soukaïna Abelhad
description:
A pitch deck says a workflow is 70% automated. Before accepting the number, Soukaïna Abelhad asks what it counts, what human work remains and who checked the result. Her first diligence test needs no model expertise: compare workload growth with the fully loaded labor required to deliver it. More output with proportionally more reviewers, trainers, escalations and rework can describe assistance rather than labor removal. A percentage without a clear denominator obscures that distinction, especially when the work called automated still depends on people to complete or correct it.

title: Tokens Are the Cheap Part — Steve Jamison, Jellyfish
description: AI spending rises dramatically while the allocated cost of a merged pull request falls. Steve Jamison explains why those observations can coexist when developer salaries and model costs are counted together. Using Jellyfish's engineering data, he reports a 60 fold increase in AI spending, 43% more merged pull requests per engineer and a 26% decline in combined cost per merged pull request over the period discussed. title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It? — Michele Grant, Leading at Scale
description: An agent's reports match the analysts' work during a pilot, yet the steering committee still has to decide whether it should operate in a core business process. Michele Grant uses an illustrative acquisition integration scenario to examine that decision. The question moves beyond technical accuracy to measurable value, accountable ownership and evidence for greater authority. A faster report is useful only if it changes a decision or releases capacity that the organization actually redeploys. title: Deploying AI Inside a Bank Is Not an Engineering Problem — Paden Gayle, Applied AI Engineers
description: A bank's document exception assistant produces a convincing demo, but security, data owners and risk reviewers still cannot approve it. Paden Gayle uses that hypothetical project to show why a working model does not establish a route into production. The missing decisions concern where the system runs, who authorized the documents, who reviews a wrong exception and which existing controls the workflow must satisfy. title: Every Building Is a Balance Sheet: Spatial Memory for Real-World Assets — Jordi Spranger, Spranic
description: Two scans of the same kitchen reveal that three chairs have moved. The change can be queried against the captured scene, with a reference back to the observation. Jordi Spranger demonstrates the idea behind Spranic's spatial memory: turn a walk through a building into a record of its objects, relationships and changes over time. A conference hall scan provides a second example. Instead of leaving the evidence scattered across photographs and PDFs, the system stores a semantic representation in a graph that can connect observations from repeat visits. title: Building Engine v2: How LangChain approaches agent improvement
description: Ben Tannyhill, Product Manager at LangChain, explains how his team builds and evaluates LangSmith Engine, the agent in LangSmith that finds issues in production traces, proposes fixes, and creates evals to catch regressions. title: Robots That Predict the Future: Dyna-2 & Physical AI — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
description:
From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung, Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. In this episode, Dyna Robotics co-founder and Chief Scientist Jason Ma joins swyx on-site to unpack how robots can learn new tasks from as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations, why predicting the future of the physical world may be the key to general-purpose robotics, and what it actually takes to build robots that work reliably for real customers.

title: How to kill your SaaS: what we learned replacing a $43K/yr tool with AI agents
description:
A SaaS vendor quoted us $43,000 a year to run speakers for my @AIdotEngineer conferences. That would be fine if it delivered the qualitySo we asked builders to clone it with coding agents, open source, eval by the people who'd actually use it: our human events team.

72 teams submitted. This is what we learned: how the best builders split work between Claude Code and Codex, why our own AI judge ranked the winner 19th, the three things almost every clone got wrong, and why owning software is a different job from building it.
